questions.question: Which of the following was a primary objective of the First Five-Year Development Plan (1957–1961) during the Imperial period in Ethiopia?

options.text: Nationalizing rural land and establishing agricultural producer cooperatives
Developing a strong physical infrastructure—particularly in transportation, construction, and communications—to link isolated regions
Decentralizing taxing authority directly to regional woredas
Dismantling all private commercial banks and state export monopolies

questions.explanation: Section 7.1.1 states that the First Five-Year Plan (1957–1961) focused on developing infrastructure (transportation, construction, and communications) to link isolated regions, creating a cadre of skilled personnel for processing industries, and accelerating agricultural development through commercial ventures.

questions.question: What main shift in development strategy was introduced in Ethiopia's Third Five-Year Plan (1968–1973) compared to the first two plans?

options.text: It shifted priority focus toward the development of the agricultural sector to address rising food shortages.
It banned all foreign direct private investment in manufacturing.
It eliminated cash crop production in favor of heavy steel manufacturing.
It abolished the feudal land tenure system throughout the empire.

questions.explanation: Unlike the first two plans that prioritized urban industrial development, the Third Five-Year Plan (1968–1973) shifted attention to the agricultural sector to combat growing food shortages and promote integrated rural development.

questions.question: What development strategy was adopted by the Ethiopian government in 1994 as the overarching foundation for long-term national economic transformation?

options.text: Export-Oriented Heavy Industrialization (EOHI)
Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization (ADLI)
Centrally Planned Collectivization (CPC)
Import-Substituting Agro-Assembly (ISAA)

questions.explanation: In 1994, the Transitional Government of Ethiopia adopted Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization (ADLI) as the national development foundation, aiming to achieve food self-sufficiency and industrial transformation through smallholder agricultural productivity.

questions.question: What is the primary definition of 'fiscal decentralization'?

options.text: The complete privatization of all state-owned commercial banks and enterprises
The devolution of taxing and spending powers from central government authorities to sub-national levels of government (regional, provincial, and municipal)
The elimination of all import tariffs on intermediate capital goods
The central bank's direct allocation of foreign exchange reserves

questions.explanation: Fiscal decentralization refers to the transfer or devolution of expenditure responsibilities and revenue-raising powers from central government to sub-national governmental units (such as regional states and municipalities).

questions.question: What long-term national vision forms the core objective of Ethiopia's Ten-Year Development Plan (2021–2030)?

options.text: Establishing a state-controlled command economy modeled on the 1970s socialist system
Making Ethiopia an 'African Beacon of Prosperity' through market-based economic reforms, private sector leadership, and institutional transformation
Nationalizing all commercial private banks and insurance corporations
Banning foreign trade in agricultural commodities

questions.explanation: The Ten-Year Development Plan (2021–2030) lays out the long-term national vision of transforming Ethiopia into an 'African Beacon of Prosperity' through sustainable growth, private-sector leadership, and institutional capacity.

questions.question: Which of the following was a major agrarian policy change introduced by the socialist Derg regime immediately following the 1974 revolution?

options.text: Nationalizing rural land, abolishing land tenancy, and putting private commercial farms under state control
Privatizing state agricultural enterprises and establishing private land titling
Eliminating compulsory grain quotas and introducing free agricultural markets
Providing tax-free holidays for foreign agribusiness investors

questions.explanation: Following the 1974 revolution, the military Derg regime nationalized all rural land, abolished feudal landlord-tenant relationships, placed commercial farms under state control, and instituted compulsory grain delivery quotas through the AMC.

questions.question: What were the four overarching development objectives articulated in Ethiopia's First Growth and Transformation Plan (GTP I, 2010/11–2014/15)?

options.text: Achieving 11% average GDP growth, expanding social access to achieve the MDGs, building a democratic developmental state, and maintaining macroeconomic stability
Nationalizing private factories, ending foreign trade, eliminating direct taxes, and closing commercial banks
Privatizing all urban residential land, devaluing currency by 500%, and banning agricultural imports
Abolishing regional administrations, reducing primary school enrollment, and eliminating domestic credit

questions.explanation: Section 7.1.3 states that GTP I was articulated through four overarching objectives: (1) maintaining at least 11% average annual real GDP growth to achieve the MDGs, (2) expanding access and quality in health and education, (3) creating a stable democratic developmental state, and (4) ensuring macroeconomic stability.

questions.question: Which of the following was a prominent structural weakness encountered during the implementation of the Growth and Transformation Plans (GTP I and II)?

options.text: Domestic private saving rates exceeded domestic investment demand by over 50%.
External debt distress worsened, inflation persisted, and the transition from low-productivity agriculture to high-productivity manufacturing remained sluggish.
The economy achieved full industrial self-sufficiency, eliminating all imports.
Urban unemployment fell to zero across all regional states.

questions.explanation: Despite rapid GDP growth, GTP I and II suffered from heavy public debt accumulation, persistent inflation, foreign exchange shortages, a widening savings-investment gap, and slow structural transformation toward high-productivity manufacturing.

questions.question: Why did the Ethiopian government domestically initiate the Home-Grown Economic Reform (HGER) program in 2019?

options.text: To re-establish a command economy with state-fixed commodity prices
To address severe macroeconomic imbalances, reduce public debt vulnerabilities, curb inflation, and transition from public-debt-led growth to private-sector-led growth
To replace the Ethiopian Birr with a regional currency
To ban domestic private enterprises from accessing commercial bank credit

questions.explanation: Section 7.2 outlines that HGER was initiated because previous rapid growth was heavily debt-financed and public-sector driven, generating acute debt distress, foreign exchange shortages, and inflation. HGER aimed to shift the growth model toward private sector leadership and supply-side productivity.

questions.question: Which of the following represents a key component of the financial sector reform under the Home-Grown Economic Reform (HGER)?

options.text: Establishing credit ceilings to permanently suppress private-sector bank borrowing
Transitioning toward market-based interest rates, establishing and expanding capital markets, and strengthening the supervisory capacity of the National Bank of Ethiopia
Abolishing all private domestic commercial banks and insurance companies
Mandating fixed official exchange rates with zero currency adjustments

questions.explanation: Section 7.2.1 specifies that HGER financial sector reforms focus on developing market-oriented financial operations, including moving toward market-based interest rates, establishing capital markets (stock exchange), and enhancing the regulatory oversight of the NBE.

questions.question: In fiscal federalism, which of the following is recognized as a major advantage of a decentralized fiscal system?

options.text: The loss of economies of scale in collecting national taxes
Interstate spillover externalities in public health and education
The ability to tailor public goods and services to local preferences and foster healthy intergovernmental competition
Ineffectiveness in executing nationwide income redistribution programs

questions.explanation: As detailed in Section 7.3.1, the core benefits of fiscal decentralization are that sub-national governments can tailor public services to local tastes and conditions, become more responsive to local citizens, and foster intergovernmental competition and policy innovation.
questions.sourceReference: Section 7.3.1, Pages 176-177 & EUEE 2017 EC, Q17 & Review Questions, Page 179

questions.question: How did the second phase of the Derg regime's economic planning (1978–1980) contrast with its immediate post-revolution phase (1974–1978)?

options.text: In 1974–1978 GDP grew by 15%, whereas in 1978–1980 the entire manufacturing sector collapsed.

In 1974–1978 political instability and nationalizations stagnated annual GDP growth at 0.4%, whereas in 1978–1980 the 'Zemecha' campaign and favorable weather fostered economic recovery, with GDP growing at 5.7% per year.
In 1978–1980 the Derg privatized all collective state farms and joined the World Trade Organization.
In 1974–1978 defense spending was completely eliminated from the national budget.

questions.explanation: Section 7.1.2 explains that in 1974–1978, nationalization dislocations and civil conflicts kept average GDP growth at just 0.4% annually. In 1978–1980, power consolidation, institutional reforms, and the Development through Cooperation Campaign (Zemecha) enabled GDP to rebound to an average annual rate of 5.7%.

questions.question: In an empirical evaluation of fiscal decentralization in a federal nation, how is the 'centralization ratio' calculated, and what does it measure?

options.text: Centralization Ratio = Central Bank Foreign Reserves / Total Money Supply (M2)
Centralization Ratio = Direct expenditure by the central government (excluding intergovernmental grants) / Total government expenditure
Centralization Ratio = Total Regional Tax Revenue / Federal Budget Deficit
Centralization Ratio = Total Public Debt / Gross Domestic Product

questions.explanation: Section 7.3 defines the centralization ratio as direct government expenditure undertaken by the central government divided by total national government expenditure (where direct expenditure excludes federal grants and transfers to sub-national units), measuring the relative fiscal weight of the central authority.

questions.question: Why does the federal government of Ethiopia make annual 'fiscal equalization grants' to regional states as an essential companion policy to fiscal decentralization?

options.text: To ensure that all regional state borders are permanently dissolved into municipal zones

To reduce regional disparities, eliminate differences in net fiscal benefits across jurisdictions, and enable less-developed regional states to deliver comparable basic public services at similar tax incidence
To finance the acquisition of commercial foreign equity shares by municipal city councils
To penalize regional states that mobilize high domestic direct tax revenues

questions.explanation: Section 7.3 notes that fiscal equalization transfers reduce disparities in net fiscal benefits among regions. Without equalization, poorer regions with smaller tax bases cannot provide basic public services (health, education, water) without imposing excessively high tax burdens on their residents.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs an Ethiopian national development framework with its respective primary focus and operational timeline?

options.text: PASDEP (1968–1973): Heavy industrial import substitution under royal council oversight
SDPRP (2002/03–2004/05): Poverty reduction via ADLI, food security, decentralization, and public-private capacity building
GTP II (1984–1994): Ten-year socialist central perspective plan under the military Derg
HGER (1957–1961): Transport corridor construction under Italian infrastructure grants

questions.explanation: The Sustainable Development and Poverty Reduction Programme (SDPRP) was Ethiopia's first full PRSP spanning 2002/03 to 2004/05, focusing on ADLI, food security, decentralization, capacity building, and civil service/justice reforms.
